0.title: Jonah: Salvation Belongs to the LORD
0.overview:
Jonah is unlike any other prophetic book. The others are collections of sermons; this is a story about a prophet, and only one of his sermons is quoted, eight words long (3:4). It is also, by turns, comic and deeply uncomfortable. Everything in it obeys God instantly, the wind, the sea, a great fish, a plant, a worm, a pagan crew, a pagan city, except the one man who knows him best.

Jonah was a real prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel. The book of Kings tells us that Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher announced that King Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25). So he preached in the eighth century BC, in the same years as Amos and Hosea, when Israel was prosperous and Assyria was rising in the east.

That matters, because God sends him to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria. The Assyrians were the terror of the ancient world, famous for cruelty; Nahum would later call Nineveh the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder (Nah 3:1). They were also the people who would one day destroy Jonah's own nation (2 Kgs 17:6). Being told to preach there was like being sent with a warning to the headquarters of an army that had burned your neighbours' villages.

Some Christians read the book as a parable rather than a record of events, because of the fish and the repentance of a whole city. Most in the Reformed tradition take it as history, chiefly because Jesus did: he spoke of Jonah in the fish and of the men of Nineveh who repented at the preaching of Jonah as real people and real events (Matt 12:39-41). These notes read it the same way, and note where the other view is held.

The story falls into four short chapters, in two matching halves. Chapter 1: God calls, Jonah runs the opposite way, and God hurls a storm at the ship. The pagan sailors pray while the prophet sleeps, and when he is thrown overboard the sea goes quiet and the sailors worship God. Chapter 2: from inside the great fish Jonah prays a psalm of thanksgiving that ends, Salvation belongs to the LORD! Chapter 3: the word comes a second time, Jonah obeys, and the whole city repents, from the king down to the cattle, so that God relents. Chapter 4: Jonah is furious, God grows a plant and kills it with a worm, and the book ends with God's question hanging in the air. In each half, outsiders respond better to God than his own prophet does.

Four themes run through the book. God rules everything. He appointed the fish (1:17), the plant, the worm and the scorching wind (4:6-8), and he hurled the wind on the sea. God's mercy reaches outsiders. Sailors worship him in chapter 1 and a pagan city turns to him in chapter 3, and this was always his purpose for Israel, to be a light for the nations (Isa 49:6). God is patient with failing servants. The word comes to Jonah the second time (3:1), and God answers his sulking with questions rather than lightning. Repentance is real when it changes conduct. Nineveh turned from the violence that is in his hands (3:8).

The heart of the book is one sentence Jonah prays in the dark: Salvation belongs to the LORD! (2:9). He means it about himself, and he is glad. What he cannot bear is that it is equally true of Nineveh. Salvation is God's to give, and he gives it to whom he pleases. That is a comfort when it comes to us and a test when it comes to people we have written off. For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8).

Jonah points to Jesus in several ways, and Jesus said so himself. One man is thrown into the storm so that others may live. Jonah is three days in the belly of the fish, and Jesus said, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40). But the differences preach as loudly as the likenesses. Jonah slept through a storm he had caused; Jesus slept in peace and then stilled the storm with a word (Mark 4:39). Jonah went into the deep for his own sin and was brought up; Jesus went into death for our sin and rose. Jonah sat on a hillside hoping a city would burn; Jesus looked at a city that had rejected him and wept over it (Luke 19:41), then suffered outside the gate to save his enemies (Heb 13:12). No wonder he said, something greater than Jonah is here (Matt 12:41).

The book ends with a question that God asks and Jonah never answers: And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city ...? (4:11). The silence is deliberate. The question was aimed first at Israel, who had the light and resented sharing it, and it is aimed now at every reader. We can be orthodox, prayerful and thoroughly biblical, and still be angry that God is kind to people we dislike. Jonah's mercy ran out at the borders of his own nation; God's did not. In heaven the song is sung to a Saviour who ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Rev 5:9). Jonah's story finishes with a question mark so that our lives may answer it.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me."<sup>3</sup>But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.<sup>5</sup>Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep.<sup>6</sup>So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."<sup>7</sup>And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.<sup>8</sup>Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?"<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."<sup>10</sup>Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.<sup>11</sup>Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous.<sup>12</sup>He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you."<sup>13</sup>Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.<sup>14</sup>Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you."<sup>15</sup>So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging.<sup>16</sup>Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.<sup>17</sup>And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Call and the Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jonah, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it (vv. 1-2). Instead, Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, going down to Joppa, paying the fare and going down into a ship (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his word to a city that deserves judgment, and his own prophet runs the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me." But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

Jonah was a real prophet in Israel's history. The book of Kings tells us that Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher announced that King Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25). Gath-hepher was a village in the north, in Galilee. So Jonah preached in the eighth century BC, in the same years as Amos and Hosea, when Israel was prosperous and Assyria was rising in the east.

That earlier message had been good news for Israel: expanded borders, national success. This message is different, and Jonah will hate it.

Some Christians read this book as a parable rather than a record of events, because of the fish and the sudden repentance of a whole city. Most in the Reformed tradition take it as history, chiefly because Jesus did. He spoke of Jonah in the belly of the fish and of the men of Nineveh who repented at the preaching of Jonah as real people and real events, and compared them to his own death and resurrection (Matt 12:39-41). These notes read it the same way. Either way, the book's message is the same, and it is aimed squarely at the reader.

"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me."

Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, founded long before (Gen 10:11-12) and later the capital of the empire. The Assyrians were the terror of the ancient world, famous for cruelty to the peoples they conquered. Nahum would later call Nineveh the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder (Nah 3:1). They were also the nation that would eventually destroy Jonah's own country (2 Kgs 17:6). Asking an Israelite to preach there was like asking someone to carry a warning to the headquarters of an enemy army that had burned his neighbours' villages.

Their evil has come up before me. (The ESV notes that this Hebrew word can mean either "evil" or "disaster", and it runs right through the book.) God has seen it. That is important: the message to Nineveh is not a pleasant one. Jonah is sent to announce judgment.

But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

God said Arise, go; Jonah rose to flee. Nineveh lay hundreds of miles to the east, overland. Tarshish lay far to the west across the Mediterranean, probably in Spain: as far in the opposite direction as a man could buy a ticket. He went down to Joppa, the port, and went down into the ship. Watch that word. Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the inner part of it (v. 5), down into the sea, and down to the roots of the mountains (2:6). Sin always has a downward staircase, and every step feels like a decision we are making freely. He even paid the fare. Running from God is never free.

What does it mean to flee from the presence of the LORD? Jonah was a prophet; he knew that God fills heaven and earth, and he says so himself in verse 9. He was not trying to find a place outside God's reach. He was resigning. He was walking out of God's service and away from the land where God had placed him. People still do this. We cannot escape God's presence, as the psalm says: If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me (Ps 139:9-10). But we can stop praying, stop meeting with God's people, and put distance between ourselves and the thing God has told us to do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and the sailors cry each to his own god while Jonah sleeps below (vv. 4-5). The captain wakes him: Arise, call out to your god! (v. 6). The lot falls on Jonah, who answers, I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land (vv. 7-9). The sailors are appalled: What is this that you have done! (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no running from God, and a believer's disobedience puts others in the storm with him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep. So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.

The first But was Jonah's (v. 3). This But is God's, and it settles the matter. God hurled a great wind, as a man hurls a spear. The storm is not bad luck; it is the pursuit of a runaway prophet by the God who will not let him go. Say it plainly: this storm is mercy. God could have let Jonah sail away.

Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep.

These were experienced sailors, and they were terrified, which tells us how bad the storm was. They did two sensible things: they prayed, each to his god, and they hurled the cargo overboard, sacrificing their profit to save their lives.

Meanwhile the one man on board who knew the true God was asleep. The contrast is deliberate and damning. Pagans pray while the prophet sleeps through a crisis he caused. Spiritual sleep is like that: the further we run from God, the less we feel the danger.

Christians cannot read this without thinking of another boat in another storm, where Jesus lay asleep on the cushion while his disciples panicked (Mark 4:38). But the two sleepers are opposites. Jonah slept in rebellion, and the storm was his fault; Jesus slept in perfect peace, and then rebuked the wind so that there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). Jonah must be thrown into the sea to save the crew; Jesus speaks and saves them all. As the disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41).

So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."

Now the captain of a pagan crew has to tell a prophet of God to pray. Notice his words: Arise, call out. They are the very words God used in verse 2, Arise, go ... and call out. God's command catches up with Jonah in the mouth of an unbeliever. It is a humbling thing when someone outside the faith shames a Christian into doing what God had already commanded.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?" And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

Casting lots was the ancient way of asking heaven a question. Normally it might mean nothing. This time God directs it exactly, as Proverbs says: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). There is nowhere left to hide. God has been closing in on Jonah through wind, waves and now a pebble in a sailor's hand.

Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?"

The questions come tumbling out. It is a strange kind of mercy that a man should be asked, in one breath, who he is and what he does, when both answers condemn him. What is your occupation? I am a prophet of God, running away from God.

And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."

Jonah's answer is perfectly orthodox and painfully ironic. He says I fear the LORD while running from him. He confesses that God made the sea and the dry land, which are precisely the two places he has been trying to use as an escape route: the sea he is sailing on and the dry land he came from. You can hold a completely correct doctrine of God and live as if none of it were true. Before we shake our heads at Jonah, we should ask what we confess on Sunday and contradict on Monday.

Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.

The sailors are more shocked by Jonah's behaviour than he is. What is this that you have done! is not really a question; it is horror. They can see what a believer half-asleep in his sin cannot: that running from the Maker of sea and land is madness.

And notice the quiet detail at the end: because he had told them. Jonah had already explained, presumably over a meal, that he was running away from God. He had made his rebellion into conversation. Sin talked about casually is still sin, and the people around us usually understand that better than we do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonah tells them, Pick me up and hurl me into the sea (vv. 11-12). The sailors row hard to save him, then pray to the LORD and throw him overboard, and the sea ceased from its raging (vv. 13-15). The men feared the LORD exceedingly and offered sacrifice (v. 16). And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God saves pagan sailors through the sin of his prophet, and saves the prophet himself by a fish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous. He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you." Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous.

He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you."

This is the first honest thing Jonah has done: it is because of me. He takes responsibility, and he offers his life to save the crew. Some read this as repentance and some as despair, a man who would rather drown than go to Nineveh. Both may be true at once. Even now he does not offer to pray for the storm to stop, or to turn the ship around and obey.

Yet God is doing something greater here than Jonah understands. One man is thrown into the deep so that many are saved, and the storm falls silent. Centuries later Caiaphas said, without knowing what he was saying, it is better for you that one man should die for the people (John 11:50). Jonah is a reluctant, half-hearted picture of the willing Saviour: Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet 3:18). The difference is that Jonah deserved the storm and Jesus did not.

Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.

Look at these pagan sailors. Rather than throw a man overboard, they rowed hard (the ESV notes the Hebrew picture is that the men "dug in" their oars), risking their own lives to save the man who had endangered them. Remember this when we come to chapter 4. The sailors do everything they can to save one Hebrew; Jonah will be furious that God saves a city. The people we write off often show more compassion than we do.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you." So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you."

Something remarkable has happened. In verse 5 each cried out to his god; now they call on the LORD, the covenant name of the God of Israel. They pray a careful prayer: do not hold us guilty of innocent blood, and they own that the storm was God's own doing: you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you. These sailors have learned more theology in one night than some learn in a lifetime.

So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging.

The third hurl of the chapter. God hurled the wind, the sailors hurled the cargo, and now they hurl the prophet. The moment he hits the water, the sea is still. God's word does not fail; when the cause of the storm is dealt with, the storm is over.

Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.

Here is the first conversion in the book, and it is pagan sailors, not Israelites. In verse 5 they were afraid of the storm; now they feared the LORD. They worship him with a sacrifice and commit themselves with vows. This is the pattern of real faith: reverence, worship, commitment.

And God did this through a disobedient prophet who never preached them a sermon. God is not limited by his servants' failures, though that is no excuse for failing. If the message of this book were "God loves Israel and judges the nations", the first chapter has already exploded it. Salvation is reaching foreigners in the middle of the sea while the prophet sinks.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

(In the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 2, as the ESV notes.) The word appointed is the key to the rest of the book. God appointed the fish here, and later he appoints a plant, a worm and a scorching wind (4:6-8). He is in command of the whole creation, great and small, and he uses all of it to deal with one stubborn man. (The ESV notes the verb may be read "had appointed", which would mean the fish was already on its way before Jonah hit the water.)

Scripture says a great fish, not a whale, and it does not tell us what kind. The point is not the biology; it is the sovereignty. The sea that Jonah used as an escape route has become God's instrument, and its creatures obey him. Amos said the same in his own way: even at the bottom of the sea God can reach a runaway (Amos 9:3).

Most importantly, this is where the swallowed prophet becomes a sign of Christ. Jesus said, just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40). Jonah went into the deep because of his own sin; Jesus went into death because of ours. Jonah was spat out on the shore; Jesus rose in glory. And Jesus added the words that should make every reader of this book tremble: something greater than Jonah is here (Matt 12:41).

Notice, finally, what the fish actually is. Jonah has just been thrown into the sea to drown, and God sends a fish. It looks like the end of him; it is his rescue. God's strangest providences are often his kindest. Many believers can look back at some dark swallowing time, the illness, the failure, the collapse, and say that it was the fish God sent to save them.

1.title: Fleeing from the Presence of the LORD
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Jonah the son of Amittai: arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before God. Instead Jonah rises to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, going down to Joppa, paying the fare and going down into a ship (vv. 1-3).

The LORD hurls a great wind on the sea until the ship threatens to break up. The sailors are afraid and each cries to his own god, throwing the cargo overboard, while Jonah lies asleep in the hold. The captain wakes him and tells him to call on his god (vv. 4-6). They cast lots, the lot falls on Jonah, and he tells them he is a Hebrew who fears the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land. The men are exceedingly afraid, for he has told them he is fleeing from God (vv. 7-10).

As the sea grows wilder, Jonah tells them to throw him into it. They row hard to reach land instead, and when they cannot, they call on the LORD not to hold them guilty of innocent blood, and throw Jonah overboard. The sea grows calm, and the men fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows (vv. 11-16). And the LORD appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, who is in its belly three days and three nights (v. 17).
1.theology:
God's call comes to his servants on his terms, and includes the people we would rather he left alone (vv. 1-2).

No one can escape God's presence; disobedience is a downward road, and it is never free (v. 3; Ps 139:7-10).

God rules wind, sea, lots and fish, and he pursues his straying servants with providences that feel like disasters and are actually mercies (vv. 4, 7, 17; Prov 16:33).

A believer's sin drags others into the storm, and outsiders often see it more clearly than he does (vv. 5-6, 10).

Correct doctrine held by a disobedient heart is worthless; faith is shown by obedience (vv. 9-10).

One man is thrown into the deep so that others may live — a dim picture of Christ, who suffered the righteous for the unrighteous (vv. 12, 15; John 11:50; 1 Pet 3:18).

God saves whom he will, even pagan sailors through a failing prophet, and the fish itself is rescue, not punishment (vv. 16-17; Matt 12:40-41).
1.examples:
A prophet buying a ticket in the opposite direction.

A believer asleep below deck while unbelievers pray.

A pagan captain telling a prophet to say his prayers.

A creed recited perfectly by a man running away from it.

Sailors digging in their oars to save the man who endangered them.

A sea that falls silent the moment God's word is obeyed.

A fish that looks like the end and turns out to be the rescue.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish,<sup>2</sup>saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.<sup>3</sup>For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me.<sup>4</sup>Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.'<sup>5</sup>The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head.<sup>6</sup>To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.<sup>7</sup>When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.<sup>8</sup>Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love.<sup>9</sup>But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"<sup>10</sup>And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Out of the Belly of Sheol
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish (v. 1). He tells how he cried to God out of my distress, and was answered (v. 2). For you cast me into the deep, with all God's breakers and waves passing over him (v. 3). Driven from God's sight, he still says, yet I shall again look upon your holy temple (v. 4). The waters closed in, weeds wrapped his head, the mountains' roots and the bars of the land shut him in, Yet you brought up my life from the pit (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: From the lowest place a believer can fall, God hears prayer and lifts him out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish, saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish,

At last Jonah prays. He would not pray on the ship, even when the captain begged him to (1:6). It sometimes takes the bottom of the sea to open a believer's mouth.

Notice two small phrases. First, the LORD his God. Jonah has run, disobeyed and been thrown overboard, and God is still his God. The relationship held when Jonah did not. Second, from the belly of the fish. There is no place so dark or so strange that prayer cannot reach God from it.

saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.

The whole chapter is a prayer, and it is mostly a song of thanks. Jonah looks back on the moment he went under the water and says that he called out and God answered.

Sheol is the Old Testament word for the realm of the dead, the grave. Jonah is saying that he was as good as dead. He had gone as low as a man can go.

Those who know the Psalms will hear them all through this prayer. In my distress I called upon the LORD ... From his temple he heard my voice (Ps 18:6). Jonah is praying in the words of Israel's hymnbook. That is what Scripture is for. When we are too frightened or ashamed to find words of our own, God's own words become our prayer, and a believer who has filled his mind with Scripture in calm days will find it there in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me. Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.' The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head. To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me.

Look carefully at who threw Jonah into the sea. The sailors picked him up and hurled him overboard (1:15), and it was Jonah's own idea. But he prays, you cast me into the deep. He sees God's hand behind the sailors' hands. They are your breakers and your waves. The psalmist had said the same: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Ps 42:7).

This is not fatalism, and it does not excuse anyone. It is the comfort of knowing that nothing reaches us except through God's hand. A Christian in a hospital bed or a collapsing business is not in the grip of blind chance.

Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.'

Here the prayer turns, on one word: yet. Jonah had tried to flee from the presence of the LORD (1:3); now, sinking, his fear is that he is driven away from your sight. We only discover how much we want God when we think we have lost him.

And then faith speaks: yet I shall again look upon your holy temple. Israelites prayed toward the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God had promised to meet his people and hear them (1 Kgs 8:38-39). Jonah believes he will stand there again. This is faith in its bare form: no evidence, no way out, simply the confidence that God will not abandon him.

The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head.

To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.

The description is vivid enough to make a reader hold his breath: water closing over his head, weeds tangled around him, sinking past the roots of the mountains. The bars are the gates of the world of the dead, shutting behind him forever. This is where Jonah's journey downward ends, which began when he went down to Joppa (1:3).

Then the second Yet: you brought up my life from the pit. The direction is finally reversed, and God is the one who reverses it. The psalm says it too: O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol (Ps 30:3). A man cannot climb back up from the roots of the mountains. He can only be carried.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Salvation Belongs to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached God's holy temple (v. 7). Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love (v. 8). Jonah promises thanksgiving and vows, and cries, Salvation belongs to the LORD! (v. 9). And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is God's to give, not ours to earn or to ration out to the people we approve of.

verseByVerse.quote: When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple. Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love. But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.

I remembered the LORD. Not that he had forgotten God's existence; he had been living as if God did not matter. Remembering, in the Bible, means turning the whole attention back to God and acting on it.

And his prayer travelled. From the bottom of the sea, inside a fish, it came to you, into your holy temple. No distance, no depth and no disgrace can block the prayer of a child of God.

Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love.

An idol is anything we trust to do for us what only God can do, and it is always vain, empty. Those who cling to such things forsake their hope of steadfast love: they walk away from the one love that would never fail them.

Jonah is right, and there is a sting in it that he may not have felt. He had just watched pagan sailors abandon their gods and worship the LORD (1:16), while he himself, who knew better, had run away. The truth we preach has a way of turning around to face us.

But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"

The prayer ends with the sentence that holds the whole book together: Salvation belongs to the LORD! It is a line straight out of the Psalms (Ps 3:8). It means that rescue is not something we achieve, arrange or deserve. It is God's, and he gives it as he pleases.

Jonah says these words in the dark, and means them about himself. In chapter 4 he will discover that they are also true about Nineveh, and he will find that much harder. It is easy to celebrate that salvation belongs to the LORD when he gives it to us; it is another thing when he gives it to people we cannot stand.

The New Testament says the same in other words: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8). And in heaven the same cry goes up from a countless crowd from every nation: Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! (Rev 7:10).

Two things stand out in this prayer. Jonah gives thanks before he is rescued; he is still inside the fish when he says it. That is real faith, thanking God for a deliverance he cannot yet see. But also, for all its beauty, the prayer never actually confesses the flight, and it never mentions Nineveh. Readers often notice that a man can pray a thoroughly biblical prayer and still be holding on to the very thing God is dealing with. Chapter 4 will show that this is exactly what has happened.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.

God spoke to the fish. He speaks, and the sea creature obeys instantly, which is more than can be said for the prophet. Everything in this book does what God says except the man who knows him best.

And the rescue is not dignified. Jonah is vomited out onto the beach, filthy and half-drowned. God's grace saves us; it does not flatter us. Many a rescued believer has had to begin again in an undignified heap, and it is still grace.

Notice also that he lands on the dry land, the very thing he had confessed God made (1:9), and the place where obedience is possible again. God brings his servant back to the beginning, and in the next chapter the call will come a second time.

Most importantly, Jesus took this chapter and made it a sign of himself: just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40). But hear the difference. Jonah prayed from the deep and was heard and lifted out. On the cross, Jesus cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46) and was not spared. He went down into death not for his own sin but for ours, and came up on the third day. Because he did, Salvation belongs to the LORD is not merely something we admire; it is something we can have.

2.title: Salvation Belongs to the LORD
2.overview:
From inside the fish Jonah prays to the LORD his God. He tells how he called out of his distress and God answered him, how he cried from the belly of Sheol and was heard (vv. 1-2). God cast him into the deep, and all God's breakers and waves passed over him; driven from God's sight, he still said he would look again on God's holy temple (vv. 3-4). The waters closed over his life, weeds wrapped his head, he sank to the roots of the mountains and the bars of the land closed on him, yet God brought his life up from the pit (vv. 5-6).

As his life was fainting away he remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached God's holy temple (v. 7). Those who cling to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love (v. 8). With the voice of thanksgiving he promises to sacrifice and to pay his vows, and cries, "Salvation belongs to the LORD!" (v. 9). Then the LORD speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah out on the dry land (v. 10).
2.theology:
God remains the God of his straying servant, and prayer reaches him from any depth (vv. 1-2, 7; Ps 18:6).

Believers may recognise God's hand behind the means that bring them low, without excusing anyone's sin (v. 3; Ps 42:7).

Faith speaks its "yet" when there is no evidence, trusting that God will not abandon his own (v. 4; Ps 31:22).

No one raises himself from the pit; salvation is God's work from first to last (v. 6; Ps 30:3; Eph 2:8-9).

Idols are empty, and those who trust them abandon the only steadfast love there is (v. 8).

Salvation belongs to the LORD, to give as he pleases, which is a comfort when it comes to us and a test when it comes to others (v. 9; Ps 3:8; Rev 7:10).

Jonah's three days in the deep are a sign of Christ, who went down into death for sinners and rose (vv. 1-10; Matt 12:40; Matt 27:46).
2.examples:
A man who would not pray on deck praying inside a fish.

Israel's hymnbook becoming a drowning man's words.

Seaweed wrapped round the head of a sinking prophet.

One word, "yet", turning a prayer around.

Thanksgiving offered before the rescue arrives.

A fish that obeys God instantly, and a prophet who does not.

Grace that saves a man and leaves him in an undignified heap on the beach.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you."<sup>3</sup>So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth.<sup>4</sup>Jonah began to go into the city, going a day's journey. And he called out, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!"<sup>5</sup>And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them.<sup>6</sup>The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.<sup>7</sup>And he issued a proclamation and published through Nineveh, "By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not feed or drink water,<sup>8</sup>but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands.<sup>9</sup>Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish."<sup>10</sup>When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Word a Second Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, with the same command and the added words the message that I tell you (vv. 1-2). This time Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, a city so great it took three days to cross (v. 3), and preached: Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown! (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives his failed servant the same commission again, and this time he obeys.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, saying, "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you." So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, saying,

Four words carry a world of grace: the second time. Jonah had refused the first call, run, been thrown overboard and swallowed. God could have found another prophet. Instead the same word comes to the same man.

Our God is the God of second commissions. Peter denied Jesus three times, and the risen Christ asked him three times, do you love me?, and three times gave him his work back: Feed my sheep (John 21:15-17). A believer who has failed badly should read this verse slowly. Failure is not the end of usefulness.

"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you."

The command is almost word for word what it was in 1:2. God has not changed his mind about Nineveh, and he has not softened the assignment to make it easier for Jonah. There is one addition: the message that I tell you. Jonah is to preach God's words, not his own. That is still the calling of every preacher, and it is a mercy, because a messenger does not have to invent the message or answer for it.

So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth.

This time Jonah arose and went. In chapter 1 he rose to flee (1:3); now he rises and obeys. It is a long walk east, several hundred miles, and it gave him a long time to think about what he was going to do.

Nineveh is called an exceedingly great city. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "a great city to God", which may mean great in God's sight, or simply very great.) The phrase three days' journey in breadth may mean the whole district of Nineveh with its surrounding towns, or, as the ESV notes, that "a visit was a three days' journey". Either way this was a vast place, and God calls it great. He notices cities, and he knows their size, their trade and their cruelty.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonah began to go into the city, going a day's journey. And he called out, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonah began to go into the city, going a day's journey. And he called out, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!"

Here is the sermon, all of it: eight words in English. There is no explanation of who God is, no invitation, no promise of mercy if they repent, not even the name of the LORD in the recorded words. Jonah walks in a day's journey and announces the end.

Forty days is a short reprieve and a long enough time to act. The word overthrown is the word used of Sodom and Gomorrah: God overthrew those cities (Gen 19:25). Every hearer would know what that meant.

Hold two things together here. First, this is a real threat, not a bluff. God does judge cities. Second, the very fact that it is announced forty days in advance is mercy. A warning is an act of kindness; a God who intended only destruction would say nothing at all.

And notice what God can do with a bare, reluctant sermon. The power is in the word of God, not in the eloquence or the warmth of the man delivering it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the people of Nineveh believed God, fasting and wearing sackcloth from the greatest of them to the least of them (v. 5). The king steps down from his throne into ashes (v. 6) and decrees a fast for man and beast, with a call to turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands (vv. 7-8). Who knows? he says (v. 9). When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: God shows mercy to the worst of cities when they turn to him, and he has the right to do so.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them. The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them.

This is a stunning sentence. A pagan city, warned by a foreign preacher with a message of eight words, believed God. Not "believed Jonah"; they took it as coming from God himself.

Their faith showed itself immediately. A fast put food aside to give the whole attention to God. Sackcloth was rough, uncomfortable cloth worn to show grief and humility. And it spread from the greatest of them to the least of them: rich and poor, powerful and powerless, together.

Keep in mind who these people were. Amos and Hosea preached for years in Israel, with God's covenant behind them, and Israel would not listen. One walk through Nineveh, and the city repents. Jesus made exactly this point: The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here (Matt 12:41). It is possible to hear the gospel all our lives and be less moved than people who hear it once.

The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

Notice the order. The people believed first, and then The word reached the king (the ESV notes it may be "had reached"). God's word ran through the streets before it reached the palace, and the most powerful man in the region did four things in one sentence: he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, put on sackcloth and sat down in ashes. Rank, dignity and comfort all went. That is what genuine repentance looks like when it reaches someone with something to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: And he issued a proclamation and published through Nineveh, "By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not feed or drink water, but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he issued a proclamation and published through Nineveh, "By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not feed or drink water,

but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands.

The king turns his personal repentance into a public policy. Even the animals are included, fasting and covered in sackcloth. To us that sounds odd, even comical, but the point is complete seriousness: nothing in the city will carry on as normal while judgment hangs over it.

Two things in the decree show that this is more than emotion. They must call out mightily to God, which is prayer in earnest, and turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Repentance that stops at sackcloth is theatre. The Assyrians were famous for violence, and the king names it. Real repentance always gets specific about what must stop, and it reaches the hands as well as the heart.

Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish."

Who knows? The king claims nothing. He has no covenant, no promise, no Bible; he has heard a sentence of doom and he throws himself on the possibility of mercy. Joel used the same words to Israel (Joel 2:14), and David said the same when his child was dying (2 Sam 12:22). This is not doubt; it is humility. God's mercy is never owed, and the person who says "Who knows?" and repents is far nearer to God's heart than the person who assumes God is obliged to forgive.

verseByVerse.quote: When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.

God saw. Not the sackcloth, not the fasting, but what they did, how they turned from their evil way. Actions proved the repentance real.

And God relented of the disaster. (The ESV notes that the word translated disaster is the same one used of Nineveh's evil in 1:2 and here; their evil brought the threat of disaster, and when the evil went, so did the disaster.)

How can God change his mind? He tells us himself: If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation ... turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it (Jer 18:7-8). This is how God has always worked. A warning carries an unspoken condition, and the warning is given precisely so that people will turn.

So God has not become unstable or changed his character. It is the Ninevites who changed, and God's unchanging character, which is gracious ... and merciful, slow to anger, means that his dealings with a repentant city must differ from his dealings with a violent one. A father who warns his child of punishment and does not carry it out when the child stops has not become unreliable; he is being exactly who he always was. As God says through Ezekiel, Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked ... and not rather that he should turn from his way and live? (Ezek 18:23).

This is where the whole book has been heading, and it is the very thing Jonah could not bear, as the next chapter will show. He was right about God, and that was his problem.

One more thing should be said honestly. Nineveh's repentance did not last for ever. A century or so later the prophet Nahum announced the city's fall, and Nineveh was destroyed. A generation turned to God and was spared; their descendants returned to the old violence and were not. Each generation must repent for itself. The message has not changed since: repent and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:15), and God commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30).

3.title: The People of Nineveh Believed God
3.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Jonah a second time with the same command: go to Nineveh and call out the message God gives him (vv. 1-2). This time Jonah arises and goes. Nineveh is an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth (v. 3). He goes a day's journey into it and calls out, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!" (v. 4).

The people of Nineveh believe God. They call a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least (v. 5). The word reaches the king, who rises from his throne, removes his robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in ashes (v. 6). He decrees that neither man nor beast shall eat or drink, that all be covered with sackcloth, that they call out mightily to God, and that everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence in his hands, saying, "Who knows? God may turn and relent" (vv. 7-9). When God sees what they do, how they turn from their evil way, he relents of the disaster he had threatened and does not do it (v. 10).
3.theology:
God restores failed servants and gives them their commission again (vv. 1-2; John 21:15-17).

Preachers are to deliver God's message, not their own, and God's word works even through a reluctant messenger (vv. 2, 4).

A warning of judgment is itself an act of mercy, since it is given so that people may turn (v. 4).

Saving faith shows itself in humility and action, and reaches the greatest and the least alike (vv. 5-6).

True repentance is specific: it turns from named sins, including violence, and it reaches the hands (v. 8).

Mercy can never be presumed upon; "Who knows?" is the right posture of a sinner before God (v. 9; Joel 2:14; 2 Sam 12:22).

God relents of threatened disaster when people turn, not because he changes, but because his unchanging character deals differently with the repentant (v. 10; Jer 18:7-8; Ezek 18:21-23).

Those who hear little and repent will condemn those who hear much and do not (v. 5; Matt 12:41; Luke 11:32).
3.examples:
A second call coming to a man who ran from the first.

A sermon of eight words with no mercy offered in it.

A whole city believing a foreign preacher it had no reason to trust.

A king stepping off his throne and sitting down in the ashes.

Cattle in sackcloth, because nothing carries on as normal.

A pagan asking "Who knows?" and finding out.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.<sup>2</sup>And he prayed to the LORD and said, "O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster.<sup>3</sup>Therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live."<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said, "Do you do well to be angry?"<sup>5</sup>Jonah went out of the city and sat to the east of the city and made a booth for himself there. He sat under it in the shade, till he should see what would become of the city.<sup>6</sup>Now the LORD God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant.<sup>7</sup>But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered.<sup>8</sup>When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."<sup>9</sup>But God said to Jonah, "Do you do well to be angry for the plant?" And he said, "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die."<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said, "You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night.<sup>11</sup>And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Prophet Who Wanted a Funeral
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry (v. 1). He prays that this is why he fled: he knew God to be a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster (v. 2). So he asks to die (v. 3), and God asks, Do you do well to be angry? (v. 4). Jonah builds a shelter east of the city and sits down to watch what will happen (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: It is possible to know God's character perfectly and resent it.

verseByVerse.quote: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. And he prayed to the LORD and said, "O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster. Therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

A whole city has just been saved, and the preacher is furious. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "it was exceedingly evil to Jonah", and that is the same word the book has used all along. In 1:2 the evil was Nineveh's. Now the evil has gone out of Nineveh and reappeared in the prophet's heart. That is a devastating turn, and it is the point of the chapter.

And he prayed to the LORD and said, "O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster.

At last we learn why Jonah ran. It was not fear of Assyrian soldiers or doubt about his calling. I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful. He ran because he was afraid God would forgive them.

What he quotes here is the description of God that the Old Testament returns to again and again, the words God spoke about himself to Moses: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). Israel sang it (Ps 103:8) and other prophets preached it (Joel 2:13). Jonah can recite it word for word, and he hates it when it is applied to the wrong people.

We are not told everything that lay behind his anger. He may have feared what Assyria would later do to his own country, which did happen. He may have felt that mercy to such a violent city was an offence against justice. He may simply have wanted to be right about the judgment he had announced. What the text says plainly is that he knew what God was like and could not bear it.

Before we judge him, let us be honest. Most of us are glad that God is merciful to us and to people like us. The test comes when God shows mercy to someone who has hurt us, or to a group we have written off. Jesus faced exactly this: This man receives sinners and eats with them (Luke 15:2), grumbled the religious people, and he answered with the story of a father and two sons, one of whom would not come in to the party (Luke 15:28).

Therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live."

Elijah once asked God to take his life (1 Kgs 19:4), and so did Moses (Num 11:15). But they were crushed by the burden of ministry. Jonah is in a temper. He would rather be dead than live in a world where God forgives Nineveh. Anger of that kind always shrinks a person's world until it contains nothing but himself and his grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said, "Do you do well to be angry?" Jonah went out of the city and sat to the east of the city and made a booth for himself there. He sat under it in the shade, till he should see what would become of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said, "Do you do well to be angry?"

God's reply is astonishing. He does not strike Jonah down. He asks him a question, as a patient teacher does, inviting him to examine his own heart: Do you do well to be angry? Is this anger right? Where has it come from?

God deals with his sulking servants far more gently than they deserve, and his questions call for an honest answer. When we are angry with God, the way back is not to pretend otherwise but to let him ask us why.

Jonah went out of the city and sat to the east of the city and made a booth for himself there. He sat under it in the shade, till he should see what would become of the city.

Jonah does not answer. He walks out, builds a rough shelter of branches on the hillside east of the city, and sits down till he should see what would become of the city. He is hoping the fire will fall after all. The forty days may not yet be over, and he means to have a good view.

Picture it: a man of God sitting in the shade, waiting for a city of more than a hundred thousand people to be destroyed. It is an ugly image, and Scripture does not soften it. One of the reasons we can trust the Bible is that it tells the truth about its heroes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — The Plant, the Worm and the Question
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God appoints a plant for shade, and Jonah is exceedingly glad (v. 6); then a worm, and a scorching wind, until he again asks to die (vv. 7-8). God asks, Do you do well to be angry for the plant? (v. 9), and presses home the lesson: Jonah pitied a plant he did not grow (v. 10). And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle? (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's compassion for people who do not yet know him is greater than his servant's, and the book ends by asking whether we share it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant. But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered. When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the LORD God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant.

God appointed again, as he appointed the fish (1:17). Here it is a plant (the ESV notes the Hebrew word probably means the castor oil plant, which grows quickly and has broad leaves). It shades Jonah's head and saves him from his discomfort (the ESV notes this may be read "his evil", the same word again).

Now comes the only time the book tells us Jonah was glad: Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant. He was exceedingly angry about a city being saved and exceedingly glad about a bush that kept the sun off his head. That is a portrait of a heart out of shape, and it is meant to make us uncomfortable. It is easy to care more about a comfortable life than about people who are perishing.

But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered.

When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."

God appoints a worm and then a scorching east wind, the dry desert wind that drains the strength out of a person. The God who commands great fish and great cities also commands a worm and a breeze. Nothing is too large or too small for his purposes.

And notice what God is doing. This is not petty revenge on a sulking prophet; it is a lesson carefully prepared. God takes away the comfort in order to expose what Jonah loves, and to give him something he actually needs more than shade.

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to Jonah, "Do you do well to be angry for the plant?" And he said, "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die." And the LORD said, "You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night. And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God said to Jonah, "Do you do well to be angry for the plant?" And he said, "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die."

God repeats his question from verse 4, now with the plant in it. This time Jonah answers, and his answer is defiant: Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die. He is absolutely sure he is in the right. That is what anger does. It supplies its own certainty.

And the LORD said, "You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night.

Here is the argument, and it is unanswerable. Jonah pitied a plant. He had not planted it, watered it or grown it; it appeared overnight and died overnight; and it existed entirely for his comfort. Yet he grieved for it.

And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?"

If Jonah can pity a plant he did not make, how much more should God pity a city full of people he did make? The phrase who do not know their right hand from their left is understood in two ways. Many take it to mean small children, which would mean 120,000 children and a much larger city besides. Others take it of the whole population: people who cannot tell right from wrong because nobody has ever told them. Either way the point stands. These are people in the dark, and God's heart goes out to them.

And then the last words of the book, which are almost comical and entirely serious: and also much cattle. God's compassion reaches even the animals of Nineveh. The God Jonah serves cares about everything he has made.

Now notice how the book ends. It ends with a question, and we never hear Jonah's answer. That silence is deliberate. The question is left hanging in the air for Israel, who were called to be a light to the nations and were sulking instead, and it hangs there for every reader. Do we share God's compassion for people who do not know their right hand from their left? Or are we more upset about our comforts than about their destruction?

The final word belongs to Jesus. A greater than Jonah came to a city that would not listen, and instead of sitting on a hill waiting for it to burn, he wept over it (Luke 19:41). He did not preach eight grudging words and withdraw; he suffered outside the gate to sanctify his people by his own blood (Heb 13:12). Jonah was thrown into the storm for his own sin, and lived; Christ went into the storm of judgment for other people's sin, and died. And he did it for enemies: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8).

That is why the church has a mission rather than a grievance. The song of heaven is sung to a Lamb who was slain and who ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Rev 5:9) — Nineveh's kind of people, and ours. The book stops at a question mark, and the answer has to come from the reader's life.

4.title: And Should Not I Pity Nineveh?
4.overview:
Nineveh's deliverance displeases Jonah exceedingly, and he is angry (v. 1). He prays that this is exactly why he fled to Tarshish: he knew God to be gracious and merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and relenting from disaster (v. 2). He asks God to take his life, saying it is better for him to die than to live (v. 3). God asks, "Do you do well to be angry?" (v. 4). Jonah goes out east of the city, makes a booth, and sits in its shade to see what will become of Nineveh (v. 5).

The LORD God appoints a plant to shade Jonah's head, and he is exceedingly glad (v. 6). At dawn God appoints a worm that withers the plant, and then a scorching east wind, so that Jonah faints and again asks to die (vv. 7-8). God asks whether he does well to be angry for the plant, and Jonah says he is angry enough to die (v. 9). God answers: Jonah pitied a plant he did not labour for, which came and went in a night (v. 10). Should not God pity Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle? (v. 11).
4.theology:
A person may know God's character exactly and still resent it when it is shown to others (vv. 1-2; Exod 34:6).

Anger at God's mercy is the sin of the elder brother, and it is found among religious people (vv. 1-3; Luke 15:1-2, 28-32).

God deals patiently with his angry servants, asking questions rather than striking them down (vv. 4, 9).

God governs great fish, plants, worms and winds alike, and uses them to teach his people (vv. 6-8; 1:17).

Hearts are exposed by what they grieve over: comfort lost, or people perishing (vv. 6-10).

God has compassion on people who are ignorant of him, and on his whole creation (v. 11; Matt 5:44-45).

The greater than Jonah wept over a city and suffered outside the gate for his enemies (vv. 5, 11; Luke 19:41; Heb 13:12; Rom 5:8-10; Matt 12:41).

The book's closing question is left unanswered so that the reader must answer it (v. 11; Rev 5:9).
4.examples:
A preacher furious that his sermon worked.

The creed of God's mercy recited as a complaint.

A man in a shelter on a hillside, waiting for fire to fall.

Exceedingly angry about a city, exceedingly glad about a bush.

A worm at dawn, and a desert wind by noon.

Pity for a plant that cost nothing, and none for a hundred thousand people.

A book that ends with a question and no reply.
